case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the one-year deadline in 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1) for obtaining an effective date back to the day after a veteran’s discharge is subject to equitable tolling.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1) (effective-date rule for disability compensation claims filed within one year after discharge), within the broader 38 U.S.C. § 5110 scheme governing effective dates for VA benefits.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The petitioner argues that § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year filing period should be equitably tolled, particularly where a veteran’s service-connected disability (including mental incapacity) prevented timely filing. He contends equitable tolling is a longstanding background principle that Congress is presumed to incorporate absent a clear statement to the contrary, and that nothing in § 5110(b)(1)’s text or structure clearly forecloses tolling. He also frames the deadline as functionally a claims-processing time limit affecting entitlement to an earlier effective date rather than a jurisdictional bar, so traditional equitable doctrines should remain available to avoid unjust outcomes for incapacitated veterans.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The respondent argues that § 5110(b)(1) is not a typical statute-of-limitations deadline but a substantive effective-date rule that defines the amount of benefits payable; as such, it is not subject to equitable tolling. The government emphasizes that § 5110 sets default effective dates and narrow statutory exceptions (including the one-year post-discharge rule), and that allowing tolling would create a judge-made exception inconsistent with Congress’s detailed scheme. It also relies on Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent distinguishing tollable filing deadlines from benefit-creating provisions that set entitlement/retroactivity limits, asserting the statute’s text, structure, and history show Congress meant to cap retroactive awards absent explicit statutory authorization.
key_precedents: Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs
Henderson ex rel. Henderson v. Shinseki
John R. Sand & Gravel Co. v. United States
Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin v. United States

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Irwin and Henderson supply the strongest case for tolling a nonjurisdictional timing rule, and that veterans’ law should avoid “traps for the unwary.” But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 5110(a)(1) is framed as a substantive cap on retroactive liability—“shall not be earlier than” the application date—departing only when “specifically provided otherwise,” and § 5110(b)(1) is one such narrow, benefit-defining departure rather than a filing bar to benefits. Brockamp and Beggerly therefore fit better than Henderson: where Congress builds a reticulated, exception-laden scheme governing payments from the Treasury, Irwin’s background presumption is rebutted because tolling would operate as a judge-made new exception expanding monetary entitlement beyond what Congress authorized. A narrow holding limited to § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year grace period preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves room for equitable doctrines in other settings where the statute does not calibrate retroactivity so explicitly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson argument is the strongest push, but it fails at the threshold because § 5110(a)(1) is not a generic procedural deadline; it is a substantive command that an effective date “shall not be earlier than” the application-receipt date “unless specifically provided otherwise,” which, as the Chief Justice notes, signals exclusivity and bars judge-made additions. Henderson’s nonjurisdictional framing (as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch explain) prevents treating certain veterans’ rules as jurisdictional traps, but it does not authorize courts to expand retroactive monetary liability beyond what Congress specifically permitted. Brockamp and Beggerly are the better analogues because § 5110 is a reticulated effective-date scheme with enumerated exceptions, and equitable tolling would function as a new exception that Congress did not enact—especially given the presence of other incapacity-related provisions elsewhere in § 5110. Under an originalist and textualist reading, the equitable appeal cannot overcome the statute’s plain limits on the Treasury’s obligation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Irwin and Henderson does not overcome § 5110’s text and structure: § 5110(a)(1) sets a substantive default that effective dates “shall not be earlier than” the application date, and departures are allowed only when “specifically provided otherwise,” making the enumerated exceptions (including § 5110(b)(1)) exclusive. As Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 5110(b)(1) functions not as a claim-filing bar but as a benefit-defining retroactivity limit; equitable tolling would expand the Government’s monetary obligation beyond what Congress authorized. Brockamp and Beggerly are more analogous than Henderson because they involve detailed, reticulated statutory limits on payments from the Treasury where judge-made tolling would disrupt a calibrated scheme. Even if the equities are strong for incapacitated veterans, the remedy must come from Congress, not from rewriting an effective-date entitlement rule into a tollable deadline.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that § 5110(b)(1) is framed as a retroactivity calibrator tied to Treasury liability, and § 5110(a)(1)’s “unless specifically provided otherwise” suggests Congress meant to enumerate departures. But under Irwin the question is whether Congress clearly displaced ordinary equitable principles, and I do not read “within one year” in § 5110(b)(1)—a simple timing condition in a uniquely pro-claimant, nonadversarial scheme—as the kind of “unusually emphatic” anti-tolling signal or dense, self-contained remedial calculus that Brockamp and Beggerly treated as incompatible with tolling. Justice Thomas’s negative inference from other express incapacity provisions is informative, yet it does not persuasively show Congress meant to foreclose equitable tolling for the one-year post-discharge rule when mental incapacity can prevent access to the system altogether; targeted statutory fixes can coexist with equitable relief for extraordinary cases. Pragmatically, a narrow tolling rule limited to truly extraordinary incapacity aligns with Henderson’s admonition against turning veterans’ benefits rules into traps for the most vulnerable while preserving administrability through a high threshold and case-specific proof requirements.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is Irwin’s presumption plus Henderson’s warning against turning veterans’ rules into “traps for the unwary,” especially where incapacity blocks access. But § 5110(a)(1)’s “shall not be earlier than … unless specifically provided otherwise” reads, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, as an exclusivity clause defining the Government’s retroactive payment obligation, not a mere deadline for filing; tolling would therefore operate as a judicially created new effective-date exception. Brockamp and Beggerly make that structural inference stronger because they treat detailed, exception-laden schemes governing payments from the Treasury as rebutting any background tolling presumption, even when the equities are substantial. Henderson’s nonjurisdictional framing helps with forfeiture and access-to-forum issues, but it does not supply authority to expand the substantive retroactivity Congress “specifically provided” in this chapter.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson argument squarely raises the equities and the general presumption favoring tolling for nonjurisdictional timing rules, but it does not defeat the specific textual signal Congress used here: § 5110(a)(1) says an effective date “shall not be earlier than” the application date “unless specifically provided otherwise,” which reads as an exclusive list rather than an invitation for equitable supplementation. As the Chief Justice explains, § 5110(b)(1) is not a bar to filing but a definition of retroactive monetary entitlement—so tolling would not merely excuse delay; it would expand the Treasury’s obligation beyond what Congress “specifically provided.” Brockamp and Beggerly are therefore more analogous than Henderson: where Congress constructs a reticulated, exception-laden scheme calibrating timing and amounts, that structure rebuts Irwin’s background presumption and leaves further exceptions to Congress. Henderson’s warning against “traps for the unwary” is important, but it cannot authorize courts to rewrite an effective-date rule that is itself the measure of substantive entitlement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson argument forcefully highlights the veteran-friendly context and the harshness for incapacitated claimants, but it still does not fit § 5110’s role in defining the Government’s retroactive payment obligation. As the Chief Justice explains, § 5110(a)(1)’s “shall not be earlier … unless specifically provided otherwise” and the chapter’s enumerated effective-date exceptions read as an exclusive, calibrated scheme; equitable tolling would operate as a judge-made new exception expanding Treasury liability beyond what Congress “specifically provided.” Brockamp and Beggerly, emphasized by Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan, are more analogous than Henderson because they counsel against importing tolling into detailed timing-and-amount frameworks with specified exceptions, and § 5110 is structured the same way. Henderson’s nonjurisdictional reasoning helps avoid jurisdictional traps, but it does not authorize courts to alter a substantive retroactivity cap where Congress has chosen the lines and elsewhere shown it can write incapacity-based relief explicitly.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Irwin supplies a presumptive availability of equitable tolling for nonjurisdictional timing rules in a veteran-friendly system, and she argues § 5110(b)(1) lacks the “unusually emphatic” anti-tolling signals of Brockamp or Beggerly. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 5110(a)(1)’s text—effective dates “shall not be earlier than” the application date “unless specifically provided otherwise”—reads as an exclusivity instruction about retroactive entitlement, not merely a procedural filing rule; tolling would operate as an extra-statutory exception expanding Treasury liability beyond what Congress “specifically provided.” Henderson’s nonjurisdictional reasoning removes a jurisdictional label, yet it does not authorize courts to revise a benefit-defining effective-date scheme that is already reticulated and exception-laden in the Brockamp/Beggerly sense. On an originalist and textualist view, the statute’s structure and Congress’s choice to enumerate particular exceptions rebut Irwin’s background presumption here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson argument remains the most powerful equitable appeal, and I agree that veterans’ procedures should not become traps for those incapacitated by service. But as the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5110(a)(1)’s “shall not be earlier than” command, coupled with the “unless specifically provided otherwise” language and the chapter’s enumerated exceptions, reads as a substantive retroactivity/payment-authorization scheme rather than a mere claims-processing deadline; that structure brings this case closer to Brockamp and Beggerly than to Irwin’s default presumption. Henderson’s nonjurisdictional framing helps avoid jurisdictional forfeiture, yet it does not supply authority for courts to create a new retroactive-effective-date exception that Congress did not “specifically provide,” especially given the administrability and fiscal consequences in a high-volume program. Under a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, the equities are real, but the remedy here is better directed to Congress than achieved by judicially expanding Treasury liability beyond the statutory design.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 5110(a)(1) establishes a default effective-date rule pegged to the date the VA receives the application, “unless specifically provided otherwise,” and § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year post-discharge provision operates as a narrow, benefit-defining exception to that default rather than a freestanding statute-of-limitations filing bar. Under Brockamp and Beggerly, the Court is reluctant to graft equitable tolling onto a “highly detailed” statutory scheme that already contains numerous specific exceptions and thereby signals Congress’s judgment about when retroactive relief is available. While Irwin supplies a general presumption of tolling for certain time limits, § 5110’s text and structure rebut that presumption by carefully cataloging when earlier effective dates are permitted, and adding a judge-made exception would undermine administrability and Congress’s calibrated choices. A narrow holding that § 5110(b)(1) is not subject to equitable tolling respects the statute’s design and preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering closely to Congress’s scheme and our precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 5110(a)(1) establishes a default effective-date rule—"shall not be earlier than the date of receipt"—and makes departures available only "[u]nless specifically provided otherwise in this chapter," indicating Congress intended the listed exceptions (including § 5110(b)(1)'s one-year post-discharge rule) to be exclusive rather than expandable by judicial equity. Section 5110(b)(1) is not a conventional statute of limitations governing whether a claim may be filed; it is a substantive limit on retroactive monetary liability that defines when benefits may begin, and equitable tolling would create a judge-made exception inconsistent with that detailed scheme. Under Brockamp and Beggerly, equitable tolling is unavailable when it is inconsistent with a statute’s text and structure, particularly where Congress has crafted a specific, reticulated set of timing rules and exceptions. The presence of an explicit incapacity-related exception elsewhere in § 5110 (e.g., § 5110(b)(4)) reinforces that Congress knew how to provide tolling-like relief and chose not to do so for § 5110(b)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 5110(b)(1) is best read not as a statute of limitations that bars a claim, but as a substantive effective-date rule that defines the extent of retroactive benefits Congress has authorized, and equitable tolling would rewrite that entitlement. The detailed structure of § 5110—establishing a default rule and enumerated, narrow exceptions including the one-year post-discharge provision—rebuts any Irwin presumption, because tolling would add a judge-made exception inconsistent with the statutory scheme. As in Brockamp and Beggerly, where Congress set precise limits on monetary relief from the Government in a detailed framework, courts should not presume equitable tolling absent clear textual room for it. Whatever the equities for incapacitated veterans, the practical consequence of allowing tolling here would be expanded retroactive liability beyond the limits Congress chose in § 5110.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 5110(b)(1)’s one-year requirement operates as a nonjurisdictional timing rule governing when a veteran may secure the special, earlier effective date (the day after discharge), and under Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs there is a rebuttable presumption that such deadlines are subject to equitable tolling absent a clear contrary statement. Nothing in § 5110(b)(1)’s text provides the kind of “unusually emphatic” or technically detailed scheme that this Court found sufficient to rebut tolling in cases like Brockamp or Beggerly; rather, the provision is straightforward and sits within a uniquely pro-claimant veterans’ benefits system. Consistent with Henderson ex rel. Henderson v. Shinseki’s recognition that veterans’ benefits procedures should not be treated as rigid traps for the unwary, equitable tolling should be available at least where service-connected mental incapacity or similar extraordinary circumstances prevented timely filing. Allowing tolling in such narrow, equitable circumstances respects Congress’s framework while preventing the harsh, real-world deprivation of benefits for the most vulnerable veterans.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5110 establishes a comprehensive, reticulated effective-date scheme: as a default, the effective date “shall not be earlier than” the application date, with specific, enumerated exceptions including § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year post-discharge rule, indicating Congress was defining the extent of retroactive entitlement rather than creating a tollable filing deadline. Under Irwin’s rebuttable presumption, the statute’s structure and the presence of tightly drawn exceptions can rebut tolling, and cases like Brockamp and Beggerly emphasize that courts should not add judge-made equitable exceptions when Congress has crafted detailed, administrable limits. Allowing equitable tolling here would effectively create a new exception to § 5110’s cap on retroactivity and undermine the workability of a benefits system that depends on bright-line effective-date rules. Henderson’s nonjurisdictional reasoning does not carry tolling across the line where Congress has specified the substantive measure of benefits payable rather than a simple claims-processing time bar.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 5110(a)(1) sets a clear default: the effective date “shall not be earlier than the date of receipt of application,” “unless specifically provided otherwise,” and § 5110(b)(1) is one of those specific, limited statutory exceptions that Congress chose to create. Treating § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year window as equitably tollable would add an atextual, judge-made exception to a detailed, reticulated scheme of effective-date rules and enumerated exceptions, the very circumstance in which this Court has declined to apply the Irwin presumption. As in United States v. Brockamp, where a technical catalog of timing/amount rules displaced equitable tolling, § 5110’s structure indicates Congress meant to define the extent of retroactive benefits and to limit them to the express exceptions it enacted. Whatever equitable appeal exists for incapacitated veterans, the separation of powers requires courts to apply the statute as written and leave any further exceptions to Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 5110(b)(1) is best read not as an ordinary claim-processing filing deadline, but as a substantive effective-date/retroactivity rule that defines the amount of benefits payable—an exception to § 5110(a)’s default rule—and courts should be reluctant to graft judge-made equitable tolling onto Congress’s carefully specified effective-date scheme. Under Irwin, a tolling presumption can apply to some federal deadlines, but it is rebutted where the statute’s text and structure show Congress meant to foreclose additional exceptions; here, § 5110 contains numerous detailed, targeted effective-date exceptions, signaling that Congress chose the circumstances for retroactive awards and left no room for judicial augmentation. Brockamp and Beggerly counsel that equitable tolling is unavailable when Congress creates a detailed, reticulated scheme with explicit exceptions, because tolling would be inconsistent with legislative design and administrability in a high-volume benefits system. Given the importance of workability and respecting the statutory lines Congress drew in § 5110, equitable tolling should not apply to § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year grace period.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 5110(b)(1) is best read, in context of § 5110’s comprehensive effective-date scheme, as a substantive limit on retroactive monetary entitlement rather than a mere claims-processing deadline; it specifies when benefits “shall” begin and thereby defines the amount payable. Where Congress has enacted a detailed framework that sets default effective dates and only narrow statutory exceptions, we are reluctant to add a judge-made equitable exception absent textual indication—an approach consistent with Brockamp’s instruction to look to statutory structure and Congress’s expressed exceptions. Irwin’s rebuttable presumption of equitable tolling is weakest when the provision functions to cap retroactive awards and when tolling would alter the substantive scope of the Government’s payment obligation, rather than merely excuse late filing in an adversarial proceeding. Given § 5110’s text and structure, equitable tolling of § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year rule would conflict with Congress’s calibrated allocation of retroactivity and thus is not available.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Although Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs establishes a rebuttable presumption of equitable tolling for certain statutory time limits, § 5110(b)(1) is best read not as an ordinary statute of limitations but as a substantive effective-date/retroactivity rule that defines the amount of benefits payable within Congress’s detailed effective-date scheme in § 5110. Consistent with United States v. Brockamp and United States v. Beggerly, the structure and specificity of the statutory exceptions in § 5110 (including the narrow one-year post-discharge rule) indicate Congress did not intend courts to add judge-made extensions through equitable tolling. Practically, while equitable concerns for incapacitated veterans are serious, creating tolling here would rework the statutory retroactivity limits and invite case-by-case expansion better left to Congress in this benefits program. Accordingly, the Irwin presumption is rebutted by § 5110’s text and scheme, and equitable tolling is unavailable for § 5110(b)(1).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the one-year deadline in 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1) for obtaining an effective date back to the day after a veteran’s discharge is subject to equitable tolling (e.g., for severe mental illness preventing timely filing).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1) (effective-date rule for disability compensation claims filed within one year of discharge), in the broader context of 38 U.S.C. § 5110’s effective-date scheme.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Arellano argued that § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year filing deadline is a classic nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule that should carry a rebuttable presumption of equitable tolling. Because Congress did not clearly preclude tolling, and because equitable tolling is a background principle used to prevent injustice where a claimant could not timely act (including due to incapacitating mental illness), courts should allow tolling so that veterans like him can receive an effective date as if the claim had been filed within one year of discharge.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Secretary argued that § 5110 does not merely set a filing deadline but defines the substantive entitlement to retroactive benefits and the limited exceptions to the general effective-date rule; as a result, equitable tolling is unavailable. In the government’s view, Congress deliberately created a bright-line, administrable scheme that tightly limits retroactivity, and allowing equitable tolling would improperly add an extra-statutory exception, undermine uniformity, and conflict with the statute’s structure and the Veterans Court/Federal Circuit precedent treating § 5110’s effective-date rules as not tollable.
key_precedents: Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs
Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin v. United States
Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson point is the hardest: § 5110(b)(1) looks like a one-year timing condition, and it is troubling if severe mental incapacity can operate as a forfeiture. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 5110(a) establishes a substantive effective-date cap (“shall not be earlier…unless specifically provided otherwise”), and § 5110(b)(1) is itself one of the specifically enumerated retroactivity authorizations—so tolling would not merely relax a claims-processing rule but would create an extra-statutory entitlement to earlier benefits. Brockamp and Auburn Regional therefore matter here: the reticulated, exception-laden design signals Congress meant the listed effective-date exceptions to be exclusive, rebutting Irwin’s background presumption even in a veteran-friendly system. A narrow holding denying equitable tolling for § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year window best respects the statute’s structure and institutional limits, while leaving any mental-incapacity accommodation to Congress or the VA within statutory bounds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Irwin and Henderson does not overcome the text Congress chose in § 5110(a)(1): an effective date “shall not be earlier” than the application’s receipt “unless specifically provided otherwise,” which makes § 5110(b)(1) a substantive entitlement carveout, not a mere claims-processing deadline. Under an originalist-textualist reading, the statute’s detailed, enumerated exceptions—highlighted by Justice Roberts and echoed by Justice Kagan—carry the negative implication that other exceptions (including equitable tolling for mental incapacity) are excluded. Brockamp’s reasoning fits: Congress built a highly reticulated, administrable effective-date scheme, and importing equity would create an extra-statutory route to retroactivity that the words “specifically provided otherwise” forbid. However sympathetic the equities, Henderson’s anti-trap principle cannot authorize courts to revise a benefits-creation provision that precisely defines when retroactive compensation is available.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Irwin and Henderson is the strongest pushback, but it mischaracterizes § 5110(b)(1) as a mere claims-processing deadline rather than a substantive limit on retroactive entitlement. The statute’s command in § 5110(a)(1)—no earlier effective date "unless specifically provided otherwise"—and the detailed, enumerated exceptions strongly resemble the scheme in Brockamp, where we refused to graft equitable tolling onto a technical, exception-laden framework. Henderson’s solicitude principle does not authorize courts to create an additional effective-date exception when Congress has already "specifically provided" the only retroactivity windows it chose to allow, and importing tolling would undermine the uniform, administrable line drawing that Justices Roberts and Kagan emphasize. However sympathetic cases of mental incapacity may be, the remedy is legislative or regulatory adjustment, not judicial enlargement of retroactive benefits beyond the text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’ Brockamp/Auburn structural point is the hardest for me because § 5110 is undeniably detailed and framed around a default rule with specified departures, and I accept that courts should hesitate before creating broad, judge-made retroactivity. But I still think the colleagues’ move—pressed by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch—to recharacterize equitable tolling as a brand-new “effective-date exception” overstates what tolling does in the Irwin tradition: it is a narrow equitable safety valve for extraordinary incapacity that prevents an otherwise impossible-to-meet filing window from becoming a forfeiture device, especially in a veteran-solicitous system Henderson tells us not to turn into a procedural trap. Brockamp involved multiple technical deadlines and administrability cues tied to mass tax refund processing; § 5110’s structure is serious, but it does not clearly speak to the narrow question whether profound mental incapacity can equitably excuse the one-year condition in § 5110(b)(1) without destabilizing the broader scheme. In my pragmatic view, denying tolling categorically here risks systematically excluding the most vulnerable veterans from the very retroactivity Congress made available for prompt post-discharge claims, and nothing in the text expressly directs that harsh result in the rare incapacity case.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson point is the hardest one: if § 5110(b)(1) were just a filing deadline, tolling for profound incapacity would fit our usual equity instincts in a veteran-friendly system. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 5110 is framed as a substantive effective-date entitlement rule—benefits “shall not be earlier” than receipt of the application “unless specifically provided otherwise”—and § 5110(b)(1) is one of the specifically enumerated carveouts, not a freestanding timing provision. Brockamp and Auburn Regional matter here because they treat a reticulated, exception-laden scheme as rebutting Irwin; tolling would operate as an extra-statutory effective-date exception, not merely a forgiving adjustment to a claims-processing rule. Pragmatically, Congress’s bright-line structure is the administrable solution in a mass system, and Henderson’s anti-trap principle cannot justify judicially enlarging retroactive entitlement beyond what Congress “specifically provided.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson point—that § 5110(b)(1) looks like a timing rule and lacks an express anti-tolling clause—squarely raises the equities for incapacitated veterans. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, § 5110 is framed as an effective-date entitlement limit: benefits “shall not be earlier” than application receipt “unless specifically provided otherwise,” and Congress then supplies a detailed, reticulated set of specific exceptions, which triggers Brockamp/Auburn Regional’s logic that courts should not add extra-textual equitable exceptions. Equitable tolling here would not merely forgive a late step in processing; it would create an additional substantive pathway to retroactive benefits beyond what Congress “specifically provided,” and that move is hard to square with a textualist separation-of-powers approach. Henderson’s solicitude principle fits procedural traps in adjudicatory review, but it cannot justify judicial enlargement of a benefits-creation provision that tightly defines when earlier effective dates are available.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—grounded in Irwin and Henderson—is that § 5110(b)(1) can be characterized as a filing-related timing rule and that denying tolling may operate as a harsh procedural trap for profoundly incapacitated veterans. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5110’s text (“shall not be earlier… unless specifically provided otherwise”) and its reticulated, enumerated effective-date exceptions make (b)(1) a substantive retroactivity authorization, not a freestanding deadline; equitable tolling would therefore function as an extra-statutory effective-date exception. Brockamp and Auburn Regional are highly relevant on that structural point: where Congress has built a detailed, administrable exceptions scheme for monetary entitlements, we generally treat that as rebutting Irwin’s background presumption. Henderson’s solicitude principle supports flexibility in procedural review rules, but it cannot justify judicially expanding Congress’s calibrated retroactive-benefits choices in § 5110, especially in a massive program where uniformity and bright lines are integral.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson point most squarely presses on our analysis, but it still does not fit § 5110’s textual architecture: § 5110(a) states a substantive cap—an effective date “shall not be earlier than” the application’s receipt—departing only when “specifically provided otherwise.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5110’s reticulated catalog of precise exceptions resembles Brockamp and Auburn Regional, where that kind of detailed scheme rebuts any background presumption of equitable tolling. Henderson’s solicitude principle targets procedural traps in appellate review and jurisdictional character; it cannot justify judicially creating an additional effective-date entitlement beyond what Congress “specifically provided.” Equitable tolling here would not merely excuse a late step; it would generate a new retroactivity exception, which the statute’s text and structure foreclose under an original public meaning approach.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Irwin/Henderson point has real moral force: a no-tolling rule can operate as a forfeiture device for profoundly mentally ill veterans. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively frame § 5110(b)(1) as part of a substantive effective-date entitlement scheme—anchored by § 5110(a)’s “shall not be earlier … unless specifically provided otherwise”—so tolling here would not merely relax a procedural step; it would judicially enlarge the retroactive-benefits authorization beyond what Congress “specifically provided.” Brockamp (and Auburn Regional) therefore matters more than I initially weighed: the reticulated, exception-laden design is strong evidence Congress meant these retroactivity windows to be exclusive, and pragmatic concerns about administrability and uniform line-drawing in a high-volume system reinforce that reading. Under my fairness-and-consequences lens, the harshness is better addressed through targeted legislative or regulatory accommodation rather than a court-created effective-date exception.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 5110 establishes a default rule that the effective date is the date VA receives the application, "[u]nless specifically provided otherwise," and then sets out a detailed set of enumerated exceptions, including the one-year post-discharge window in § 5110(b)(1). That kind of highly reticulated, benefits-limiting scheme is strong evidence Congress did not leave room for an additional, extra-statutory exception through equitable tolling, rebutting any Irwin presumption. As in Brockamp and Auburn Regional, where Congress crafted specific timing and retroactivity rules with limited exceptions, importing equitable tolling would undermine the statute’s administrable line-drawing and the uniformity of effective-date determinations. A narrow ruling denying tolling here respects the statutory structure and precedent while leaving any hardship-based adjustment to Congress rather than judicial supplementation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of 38 U.S.C. § 5110 establish a substantive effective-date entitlement with a general rule and tightly drawn exceptions, including § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year window for an effective date back to the day after discharge; courts may not add an extra-statutory equitable exception. Like the “highly detailed” and “technical” scheme in United States v. Brockamp, § 5110 contains an enumerated catalog of specific effective-date provisions that strongly indicates Congress foreclosed unwritten tolling doctrines. Even assuming Irwin’s background presumption could apply in some benefits contexts, § 5110’s exception-laden design rebuts it by demonstrating that Congress chose administrable bright lines rather than case-by-case equitable inquiries. Under a textualist approach, the remedy for harsh results—including those arising from mental incapacity—lies with Congress, not judicial revision of § 5110’s effective-date scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 5110(a)(1) sets a clear default rule that the effective date “shall not be earlier than the date of receipt of application” “unless specifically provided otherwise,” and § 5110(b)(1) supplies a narrow, congressionally drawn one-year exception for claims filed within a year of discharge. That structure is a detailed, exception-laden scheme defining the scope of retroactive entitlement, leaving no textual room to add an extra-statutory equitable-tolling exception, much like the limitations Congress crafted in United States v. Brockamp. Even assuming Irwin’s general presumption could apply, § 5110’s design and administrability concerns rebut it by indicating Congress intended bright-line effective-date rules with exclusive statutory exceptions. Allowing equitable tolling here would expand retroactivity beyond what Congress “specifically provided,” undermining uniformity and imposing serious administrative burdens in a high-volume benefits system.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 5110(b)(1) functions as a nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule that governs when a veteran may obtain a more favorable effective date, and under Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs there is a rebuttable presumption that such time limits are subject to equitable tolling absent a clear statement to the contrary. Henderson v. Shinseki instructs that veterans’ benefits provisions should not be read to erect harsh procedural traps inconsistent with Congress’s solicitude for veterans, especially where severe mental illness can make timely filing impossible. Although the Government invokes United States v. Brockamp to argue that § 5110’s detailed exceptions foreclose tolling, the text of § 5110(b)(1) contains no express anti-tolling language, and equitable tolling would operate as a narrow safety valve to prevent manifest injustice for incapacitated veterans without rewriting the overall effective-date scheme. Given the practical impact on vulnerable claimants, equitable tolling should be available in extraordinary circumstances such as profound mental incapacity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5110(a)(1) sets a clear default effective-date rule (date VA receives the application) and then permits earlier dates only when "specifically provided otherwise," with § 5110(b)(1) supplying a narrow, one-year post-discharge exception. Under Brockamp, the Irwin presumption of equitable tolling is rebutted when Congress creates a highly reticulated, administrable, exception-laden scheme that would be destabilized by case-by-case equitable additions; § 5110’s detailed list of effective-date exceptions, including the distinct disability-related carveout in § 5110(b)(4), strongly indicates Congress chose the limits of retroactivity. This provision functions less like a simple claims-processing deadline (cf. Henderson) and more like a substantive condition on the extent of retroactive entitlement, and equitable tolling would effectively create an extra-statutory effective-date exception. Given the statutory structure and need for uniform, workable administration in the VA benefits system, tolling is inconsistent with the text and design of § 5110.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 5110 establishes a default effective-date rule—“the date of receipt of the application”—and then enumerates specific, tightly drawn exceptions “unless specifically provided otherwise,” 38 U.S.C. § 5110(a)(1), including the one-year post-discharge provision in § 5110(b)(1). That structure looks less like a freestanding claims-processing deadline and more like a substantive limit on retroactive entitlement, and importing equitable tolling would add an extra-textual exception Congress did not “specifically provide.” Under Brockamp, the Irwin presumption is rebutted where Congress has crafted a detailed, exception-filled timing scheme that signals no room for equitable additions; § 5110’s comprehensive set of effective-date rules and exceptions fits that pattern. However sympathetic the equities, the separation-of-powers problem is that tolling here would revise the benefit Congress authorized rather than merely excuse a procedural misstep.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 5110 establishes a comprehensive effective-date scheme in which the one-year provision in § 5110(b)(1) operates not as a freestanding limitations period but as a tightly cabined exception to the general rule in § 5110(a) that benefits run from the claim’s filing date. Under Brockamp and Auburn Regional, the Irwin presumption of equitable tolling is rebutted where Congress has created a detailed, exception-laden benefits framework and adding judge-made tolling would disrupt administrability and uniformity—concerns that are acute in VA effective-date determinations. The statute’s structure (specific, enumerated exceptions to retroactivity) and longstanding treatment of effective-date rules as fixed counsel judicial restraint and adherence to Congress’s bright-line rule, leaving any mental-illness accommodation to legislative or administrative action rather than equitable alteration by courts. Accordingly, equitable tolling should not apply to § 5110(b)(1)’s one-year deadline.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 5110 establishes a substantive effective-date scheme: the default rule in § 5110(a) ties the effective date to the application’s receipt, and § 5110(b)(1) is a limited statutory exception allowing an earlier date only if the claim is filed within one year of discharge. The text and structure—especially § 5110’s numerous, detailed, technical exceptions—strongly indicate Congress chose specific circumstances for retroactivity and left no room for courts to add an extra-statutory equitable-tolling exception, akin to the “highly detailed” time-and-exceptions scheme that rebutted tolling in United States v. Brockamp. Even assuming Irwin’s presumption might apply to some nonjurisdictional deadlines, equitable tolling is unavailable where inconsistent with the statute’s design, and § 5110(b)(1) functions as a condition on obtaining a special, earlier effective date rather than a freestanding claims-processing deadline. Precedent in related contexts likewise treats detailed benefits/administration schemes as rebutting tolling when Congress has specified the permissible departures from a general rule (see Brockamp; Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 5110(b)(1) operates not as a freestanding claims-processing deadline but as a limited, substantive exception to § 5110(a)’s default rule that the effective date is no earlier than the date VA receives the application, and § 5110 as a whole contains a detailed catalog of specific, technical exceptions that reflects Congress’s considered choices about retroactivity. Under Brockamp, that kind of “highly detailed” exception-laden scheme supplies “good reason” to conclude Congress did not intend courts to add an extra-statutory equitable-tolling exception, even if Irwin’s general presumption might otherwise apply. Henderson supports reading veterans’ statutes with an eye toward fairness and nonjurisdictional flexibility, but it does not authorize courts to rewrite an explicit effective-date scheme that tightly limits retroactive awards. Given the statutory structure and the administrability/uniformity interests Congress appears to have embedded in § 5110, equitable tolling is unavailable here.
